claims.claim: Hobb says that in a short story she cuts everything that does not describe the setting, advance the plot or give a character insight.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Other Fantasy (OF Blog, Larry Nolen), 2003
claims.quote: cut out everything that does not describe the setting

claims.claim: Hobb states that her prose written as Megan Lindholm is much leaner than her prose written as Robin Hobb.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Other Fantasy (OF Blog, Larry Nolen), 2003
claims.quote: Prose as Megan Lindholm is much leaner than prose as Robin Hobb

claims.claim: Hobb says that in a novel she sprawls, and knows she does.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Other Fantasy (OF Blog, Larry Nolen), 2003
claims.quote: In a novel, I sprawl, and I know it

claims.claim: Hobb tells aspiring writers to make the economy and geography of an invented place make sense.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Other Fantasy (OF Blog, Larry Nolen), 2003
claims.quote: Make your economy and geography make sense

claims.claim: Hobb gives as an error of scale the idea that a tiny village would support an artisan who specialises in doorknockers.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Other Fantasy (OF Blog, Larry Nolen), 2003
claims.quote: A tiny village isn't going to have an artisan

claims.claim: Hobb gives as an error of labour scale the idea that a medieval farm family harvested its entire farm in one afternoon.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Other Fantasy (OF Blog, Larry Nolen), 2003
claims.quote: A medieval farm family didn't harvest its entire farm in one afternoon

claims.claim: Hobb says every character, however small the part, is the main character while on stage.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Other Fantasy (OF Blog, Larry Nolen), 2003
claims.quote: Every character is the main character

claims.claim: Hobb says that inside a villain's skin the villain is wondering what is for dinner tonight.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Other Fantasy (OF Blog, Larry Nolen), 2003
claims.quote: even the villain is wondering what is for dinner tonight

claims.claim: Hobb names immediacy and reader identification as the benefits she found in writing Farseer in first person.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Other Fantasy (OF Blog, Larry Nolen), 2003
claims.quote: Immediacy and reader identification

claims.claim: Hobb says first person confined her to telling the reader only what Fitz knew at that moment.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Other Fantasy (OF Blog, Larry Nolen), 2003
claims.quote: I could only tell the reader what Fitz knew at that moment

claims.claim: Hobb calls the first person voice the natural voice for the story teller.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Aidan Moher, A Dribble of Ink, 2007
claims.quote: the first person voice is the natural voice for the story teller
claims.routeHint: WebFetch returned HTTP 403; curl with browser user agent returned the page

claims.claim: Hobb says first person makes the reader privy to the viewpoint character's innermost thoughts and feelings.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Aidan Moher, A Dribble of Ink, 2007
claims.quote: the reader is privy to the characters innermost thoughts and feelings

claims.claim: Hobb says that writing as Hobb she tends to write longer, more detailed stories.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Aidan Moher, A Dribble of Ink, 2007
claims.quote: I tend to write longer, more detailed stories
claims.page: Q on the two pen names

claims.claim: Hobb says the Lindholm writing style is not as leisurely as the Hobb style.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Aidan Moher, A Dribble of Ink, 2007
claims.quote: The Lindholm writing style is not as leisurely
claims.page: Q on the two pen names

claims.claim: Hobb says that when her characters are hurt they acquire baggage that may later affect what they do.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Aidan Moher, A Dribble of Ink, 2007
claims.quote: they acquire baggage and later on it may affect what they do

claims.claim: Hobb says the reader drags the character's accumulated baggage through the reading.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Aidan Moher, A Dribble of Ink, 2007
claims.quote: he drags that same baggage through the reading

claims.claim: Hobb says she often had to trust the reader to make a leap the narrator did not make.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Aidan Moher, A Dribble of Ink, 2007
claims.quote: I often had to trust that the reader would make a leap
claims.page: Q on first vs third person

claims.claim: Hobb says she coped with first-person limits in Farseer by putting little prologues at the beginning of each chapter that gave the reader additional information.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Aidan Moher, A Dribble of Ink, 2007
claims.quote: little prologues at the beginning of each chapter
claims.page: Q on first vs third person

claims.claim: Hobb says there is a fairly clean dividing line between the Robin Hobb voice and the Megan Lindholm voice in her writing.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, Locus Magazine interview excerpts, December 2005
claims.quote: a fairly clean dividing line between the Robin Hobb voice

claims.claim: Hobb describes her own writing style as both leisurely and intimate.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Robert Thompson, Fantasy Book Critic, January 2008
claims.quote: I would describe my writing style as both leisurely and intimate

claims.claim: Hobb says characterisation for her means putting in details and incidents that may not directly move the plot forward.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Robert Thompson, Fantasy Book Critic, January 2008
claims.quote: details and incidents that may not directly move the plot forward

claims.claim: Hobb says the pacing at the beginning of any of her books is usually a lot slower than towards the end.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Robert Thompson, Fantasy Book Critic, January 2008
claims.quote: The pacing at the beginning of any of my books is usually

claims.claim: Hobb attributes her slow openings to so many words being given over to character construction.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Robert Thompson, Fantasy Book Critic, January 2008
claims.quote: so many words are given over to character construction

claims.claim: Hobb illustrates unearned consequence with a two-sentence summary of a friend killing a friend, saying it reads more like a joke than a devastating occurrence.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Robert Thompson, Fantasy Book Critic, January 2008
claims.quote: That seems more like a joke than a devastating occurrence

claims.claim: Hobb says that when she propelled the reader directly into a scene without building up to it, the scene lacked the impact she wanted.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Robert Thompson, Fantasy Book Critic, January 2008
claims.quote: when I propelled the reader directly into it, it lacked the impact

claims.claim: Hobb says her story is really about how the events affect the characters rather than about the events themselves.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Patrick St-Denis, Pat's Fantasy Hotlist, 2005
claims.quote: how the events affect the characters rather than about the events

claims.claim: Hobb describes each sentence as narrowing an infinite number of possibilities down to a single track.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Patrick St-Denis, Pat's Fantasy Hotlist, 2005
claims.quote: With every sentence, you narrow an infinite number of possibilities

claims.claim: Hobb says some characters speak in longer sentences and some in shorter ones, as a way of differentiating them.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, speaking on Writing Excuses 11.Bonus-01 (Oct 2016), fan transcript at wetranscripts
claims.quote: Some characters speak in longer sentences, some speak in shorter sentences
claims.confidence: medium; a listener-made transcript of a podcast, not an author-checked text

claims.claim: Hobb says differentiating characters is a choice of vocabulary and a way of seeing things.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, speaking on Writing Excuses 11.Bonus-01 (Oct 2016), fan transcript at wetranscripts
claims.quote: it's a choice of vocabulary, it's a way of seeing things

claims.claim: Hobb gives her own household as an example of occupational vocabulary, where a sailor's galley, head and deck name the same rooms as her kitchen, bathroom and floor.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, speaking on Writing Excuses 11.Bonus-01 (Oct 2016), fan transcript at wetranscripts
claims.quote: we have a galley, we have a head, we have a deck

claims.claim: Hobb proposes a test in which the reader of a passage of dialogue should be able to tell who is speaking without the attribution tags.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, speaking on Writing Excuses 11.Bonus-01 (Oct 2016), fan transcript at wetranscripts
claims.quote: able to tell who is talking without all the little clues

claims.claim: Hobb says that what an assassin notices on entering a room differs from what a child entering the same room notices.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, speaking on Writing Excuses 11.Bonus-01 (Oct 2016), fan transcript at wetranscripts
claims.quote: if you are an assassin and you walk into the room

claims.claim: Hobb says the biographical details filled in around a character build the world at the same time.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, speaking on Writing Excuses 11.Bonus-01 (Oct 2016), fan transcript at wetranscripts
claims.quote: details that fill in around the character build the world

claims.claim: Elliott describes the first paragraph of Assassin's Apprentice as an excerpt from a piece being composed inside the story's own world.
claims.source: Geoffrey B. Elliott, 'A Robin Hobb Rereading Series-Entry 1', Elliott RWI, 2019
claims.quote: an excerpt from a piece being composed within the milieu

claims.claim: Elliott names Hobb's habit of opening chapters with in-world reference materials an Asimovian move.
claims.source: Geoffrey B. Elliott, 'A Robin Hobb Rereading Series: Entry 226', Elliott RWI, 2021
claims.quote: the Asimovian move of grounding chapters in in-milieu reference materials

claims.claim: Elliott, writing as a medievalist, says the chapter-opening passage enacts the piecing-together of disparate and not always complete sources.
claims.source: Geoffrey B. Elliott, 'A Robin Hobb Rereading Series: Entry 226', Elliott RWI, 2021
claims.quote: the piecing-together of disparate and not always complete sources

claims.claim: The reviewer says Hobb takes a cliched epic-fantasy plot point and fleshes it out with motivations and characters and consequences until it looks realistic.
claims.source: Vacuous Wastrel (pseudonymous reviewer), 'The Golden Fool, by Robin Hobb', 2013
claims.quote: fleshes it out with motivations and characters and consequences

claims.claim: The reviewer says Hobb tells a standard heroic plot from an unexpected, peripheral perspective and thereby gives the realistic inner workings of the myth.
claims.source: Vacuous Wastrel (pseudonymous reviewer), 'The Golden Fool, by Robin Hobb', 2013
claims.quote: the realistic inner workings of the myth

claims.claim: The reviewer identifies worrying about the apprentice fees for dependants as the kind of domestic matter most epic fantasy does not spend pages on.
claims.source: Vacuous Wastrel (pseudonymous reviewer), 'The Golden Fool, by Robin Hobb', 2013
claims.quote: worrying about the apprentice fees for dependants

claims.claim: The reviewer says the book insists that motivations are personal and that consequences will also be personal.
claims.source: Vacuous Wastrel (pseudonymous reviewer), 'The Golden Fool, by Robin Hobb', 2013
claims.quote: that motivations are personal, and that consequences will also be personal

claims.feature: other: fantastic subordinated to the ordinary
claims.claim: The reviewer says the book reminds the reader that the fantasy only matters because of the reality in its shadow.
claims.source: Vacuous Wastrel (pseudonymous reviewer), 'The Golden Fool, by Robin Hobb', 2013
claims.quote: the fantasy only matters because of the reality in its shadow

claims.claim: The reviewer says Hobb builds tense scenes out of characters watching each other's expressions, so that much is accomplished with only glances.
claims.source: Vacuous Wastrel (pseudonymous reviewer), 'The Golden Fool, by Robin Hobb', 2013
claims.quote: So much can be accomplished with only glances

claims.claim: The reviewer judges that Hobb's prose is usually unremarkable, locating her effect elsewhere than in sentence beauty.
claims.source: Vacuous Wastrel (pseudonymous reviewer), 'Dragon Keeper, by Robin Hobb', 2014
claims.quote: As is usually the case with Hobb, her prose is unremarkable

claims.claim: The reviewer judges Hobb's prose solid and effective and occasionally pretty, but not award-winning for beauty.
claims.source: Vacuous Wastrel (pseudonymous reviewer), 'Fool's Fate, by Robin Hobb', 2013
claims.quote: prose is solid and effective and occasionally pretty

claims.claim: The reviewer describes Hobb's language as having a slightly heavy and old-fashioned tone common to the genre.
claims.source: Vacuous Wastrel (pseudonymous reviewer), 'Fool's Quest, by Robin Hobb', 2015
claims.quote: that slightly heavy and old-fashioned tone common to the genre

claims.claim: Dean says Hobb has created a number of small intimate settings centred around her characters.
claims.source: Christopher Luke Dean, 'The Greatest Fictional World Builders: Robin Hobb', Writers Write, 2020
claims.quote: created a number of small intimate settings centred around her characters

claims.claim: Dean says Hobb makes her readers care for her setting as much as her characters.
claims.source: Christopher Luke Dean, 'The Greatest Fictional World Builders: Robin Hobb', Writers Write, 2020
claims.quote: make her readers care for her setting as much as her characters

claims.claim: Dean says Hobb's characters grow or die or get worse rather than remaining stable.
claims.source: Christopher Luke Dean, 'The Greatest Fictional World Builders: Robin Hobb', Writers Write, 2020
claims.quote: Her characters grow or die or get worse
